  • Two bugs that were found and fixed, now covered by regression tests: a bare except used to turn failing descriptor calculations into six silent zeros, and an empty string was parsed by RDKit as a valid empty molecule and produced a nonsense prediction. A test requires real descriptors for a valid molecule, and another requires that a failing scaling step is reported as an error.
  • Prediction: the output is a finite number in a sane range, and different molecules give different predictions (this guards against predicting on a constant input).
  • Interpretation: every logP category and the bucket boundaries.

Not covered

  • The model's accuracy: tests check that the pipeline works, not that R² stays at 0.90. There is no test that retrains the model.
  • Chemical plausibility of single predictions: there is no comparison with reference logP values for known molecules.
  • The Streamlit interface and the deployed demo: there are no automated tests for them.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The numbers above come from one held-out test split of a single PubChem dataset. No scaffold-based split and no external dataset are reported, so how the model behaves on a new chemical series is not measured.
  • The labels are the PubChem logP values (experimental and computed), so the model inherits whatever noise they carry.
  • A point prediction only: no uncertainty estimate and no applicability-domain check (the Drug Solubility Predictor has both).

Tech stack: Python, PyTorch, RDKit, scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, Streamlit, pytest, GitHub Actions.

Related: the Drug Solubility Predictor solves a neighbouring task (a single-molecule property from RDKit features, with Random Forest and uncertainty estimates). The Buchwald-Hartwig C-N Coupling Optimizer uses the same cheminformatics toolkit for reaction yield instead of a molecule property.

docs.title: 🚶 People Counter
docs.text:
Local, CPU-only person detection and directional counting — deep-learning object detection plus multi-object tracking, wrapped in an interactive Streamlit app.

Live demo: people-counter-yolox.streamlit.app · GitHub Repository

Video mode — each tracked person keeps a stable ID across frames; the magenta line is a configurable counting gate (IN / OUT / NET).

Image mode — one-shot detection with per-box confidence scores.

docs.title: Why this project
docs.text:
The portfolio previously had a "Person Counter" that was actually a Haar-Cascade face counter mislabeled as a person counter — it couldn't count anyone facing away from the camera, and wasn't a real detector at all. I rebuilt it from scratch as an actual person detector (YOLOX-nano, deep learning) with multi-object tracking, instead of quietly patching the old one.

Together with the Erythrocyte Shape Analyzer, this shows two different ends of my computer vision work: classical image processing there (Otsu thresholding, contour detection, ellipse fitting), versus a modern deep-learning object detector plus a multi-object tracker here. It's also a useful contrast with the Cuneiform Sign Classifier: that project classifies an already-cropped image, while this one has to first find and localize every person in the frame before anything else can happen. The Emotion Recognition project sits one step further down that pipeline: it takes an already-detected face and classifies the expression with a fine-tuned ResNet18 (and still uses a Haar Cascade for the detection step, the technique the old Person Counter was built on).

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Image mode — upload a photo, get back per-person bounding boxes with confidence scores and a total count.
  • Video mode — upload a clip, draw a counting line anywhere in the frame, and get IN/OUT/NET counts of people crossing it, with each tracked person keeping a stable ID across frames.

A bundled sample image and video let a visitor try both modes without needing their own file.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Detection: YOLOX-nano (COCO-pretrained, ONNX export), run locally via ONNX Runtime on CPU. Only the "person" class is kept.
  • Tracking (video mode): trackers's ByteTrackTracker, associating detections frame-to-frame by IoU.
  • Line-crossing counting: a small, pure-Python module that watches which side of a user-drawn line each tracked person's centroid is on, and counts a crossing whenever that side flips — independent of any CV/ML code, unit-tested with synthetic positions, no video or model weights required.

docs.title: Measured accuracy
docs.text:
Evaluated against a real labeled sample (62 people-containing images from the public coco128 dataset), matching detections to ground-truth boxes at IoU ≥ 0.5 — numbers are regenerated from scratch by evaluate.py, not estimated:

Metric Value Precision 0.825 Recall 0.520 F1 0.638 CPU inference speed ~95 FPS (10.5 ms/image)

docs.title: Data security & privacy
docs.text: All inference runs locally — no image or video is ever sent to a third-party API. Uploaded video is written to a private temp file only because OpenCV needs a real file path to read it, and that file is deleted immediately after processing, even if something goes wrong. Nothing uploaded is logged, stored, or kept between requests.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Automated tests run on every push and pull request (pytest in GitHub Actions). All tracking and line-crossing logic is tested with synthetic, injectable detectors, so the suite needs no video, no images and no model weights.

What is verified

  • Line-crossing counting: the pure-Python counter is driven with synthetic positions: a crossing is counted when the side of the line flips.
  • Video pipeline: the wiring of detector, tracker and counter is tested with a fake detector (FakeDetector).

Not covered

  • Detection accuracy in CI. Precision, recall and speed are measured separately by evaluate.py on the public coco128 sample; CI does not run it.
  • Counting accuracy on real video. The IN/OUT counts were not compared with manually counted ground truth.
  • The ONNX model itself, real video files and the Streamlit interface in a browser.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Recall is the honest weak point. YOLOX-nano is the smallest model in its family (built for speed over accuracy) and struggles most on dense crowd scenes with many small, overlapping people. A larger YOLOX variant would trade some CPU speed for materially better recall.
  • The counting line only works if it's oriented against the actual direction of motion in the video. A camera looking across a path (people moving left/right) needs a vertical line; a camera looking down a corridor (people moving toward/away from camera) needs a horizontal one. There's no universally-correct default — this is why the line is configurable with sliders rather than fixed.
  • Free-tier CPU-only hosting means very long or very high-resolution video uploads are capped (frames are downscaled before processing, and there's a hard length limit) to avoid exhausting the host's memory.- The evaluation uses a small public image sample (coco128), not surveillance-style video, so the accuracy figures describe detection on still images and say nothing about counting on a specific camera.

Tech stack: Python, Streamlit, ONNX Runtime, OpenCV, trackers (ByteTrack), supervision, imageio-ffmpeg, pytest, GitHub Actions. License: code MIT, YOLOX-nano weights Apache 2.0.

docs.title: 🌈 Raman Spectroscopy Analyzer
docs.text:
A Streamlit app that takes a raw Raman spectrum through baseline correction, normalisation, smoothing, peak detection and peak fitting, and exports the results, with a focus on carbon materials such as carbon nanotubes and graphene.

GitHub Repository · Live demo (Streamlit)

docs.title: Why this project
docs.text: Analysing a Raman spectrum of a carbon material means a baseline, a normalisation, a peak table and then the ratio of the D and G bands as a measure of defects. Each step involves a choice that changes the final number. This tool puts the whole chain in one app, shows the result of every step on a plot, and applies the same settings to many files at once.

docs.title: Results at a glance
docs.text:
The tool does not produce a model score. What it gives is a processed spectrum and a table:

Step Options Baseline Linear (endpoints), Asymmetric Least Squares Normalisation Min-Max, maximum intensity, area, vector (L2) Smoothing Savitzky-Golay (optional) Peak fitting Lorentzian, Gaussian, Pseudo-Voigt (bounded least squares with parameter uncertainties from the covariance matrix) Quantities ID/IG, I2D/IG, crystallite size La from the Tuinstra-Koenig relation Export CSV (spectrum, peaks, fit), XLSX, a TXT report, and a ZIP for batch runs

Example: a sample CNT-COOH spectrum of 7,070 points between 603 and 3,400 cm⁻¹; on another sample spectrum, automatic peak detection (minimum height 0.15, prominence 0.08) finds 11 peaks.

docs.title: What the tool shows
docs.text:
• Background removal exposes the carbon bands. On the sample spectrum the D, G and 2D bands are clearly resolved once the fluorescence background is subtracted; the app plots the raw spectrum with the fitted baseline and the corrected spectrum below it.
  • The excitation wavelength enters the crystallite size. The Tuinstra-Koenig relation depends on the laser wavelength (458–785 nm), so it is a parameter of the app and not a hardcoded constant.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Specification first. SPEC.md describes the architecture, the reason for each dependency version and the data-security rules. A first version was deleted and rebuilt from scratch under this specification after repeated deployment crashes.
  • Logic apart from the interface. The Streamlit file only orchestrates; loading and validation, preprocessing, peak detection and fitting, visualisation, export and batch processing are separate modules that tests can call without a browser.
  • Input validation: one file or several .txt files with two columns (wavenumber, intensity), checked on load.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
65 automated tests run on every push (pytest in GitHub Actions).

What is verified

  • Each module of the logic layer: data loading and validation, preprocessing, peak detection, peak fitting, export and batch processing.

Not covered

  • Agreement with reference values. No comparison with other Raman software or with published ratios for the sample spectra is documented, so the tests show that the code runs as designed, not that the numbers match another tool.
  • The Streamlit interface and the interactive charts.
  • Spectra of materials other than the carbon samples used during development.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The Tuinstra-Koenig relation was derived for graphitic carbons. For nanotube samples the crystallite size from ID/IG is an indication, not a measurement.
  • I2D/IG as a layer count applies to graphene; for nanotubes it should be read with the same care.
  • The sample data are three CNT-COOH spectra; the behaviour on noisy or strongly fluorescent spectra of other materials was not evaluated.

Tech stack: Python, Streamlit, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Plotly, Matplotlib, pytest, GitHub Actions.

Related: the same carbon-nanotube topic is covered by the Carbon Nanotube Visualizer (structure and electronic properties) and the Carbon Nanotubes RAG System (questions over the research literature).

docs.title: 🤖 Scientific Research Agent
docs.text:
A tool-using LLM agent (LangChain and LangGraph) that answers scientific questions by choosing between Wikipedia, ArXiv, PubMed and a safe calculator, hardened for a public demo and tested without an API key.

GitHub Repository · Spec and threat model · Live demo (Streamlit) · Evaluation code and raw results

docs.title: Why this project
docs.text: An agent that can call tools is easy to demo and easy to get wrong in public: the model may pick the wrong tool, a calculator tool may execute arbitrary code, a visitor may run up the token bill, and one visitor may see another's history. This project builds a small research agent with these problems handled and measured: safe calculation, usage limits, per-session data, source links under each answer, and an evaluation harness with a held-out split. Answer quality is only partly measured (tool choice, calculator, safety, sources on a small dev set); the factual quality of free text is not.

docs.title: Results at a glance
docs.text:
Dev set: 16 of the 32 hand-written cases, gpt-4o-mini, one real run.

Measure Result Tool choice 14/14 (95% CI 0.79–1.00) Calculator correctness 3/3 Safety behaviour 2/2 Sources shown 10/10 Cost about 1,000 tokens and 5.5 s per question

The test split has not been run yet, and with 16 cases the intervals are wide. Treat these numbers as a smoke check, not a benchmark.

docs.title: What the evaluation showed
docs.text:
• The harness separates tuning from judging. Cases are split into dev (for tuning) and test (run once per configuration, which the runner enforces), and a test checks that no evaluation question leaks into the prompt or code. Results are published only after a real run.
  • What a visitor gets next to the answer: links to the pages and papers the tools actually retrieved, and the agent's reasoning steps.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
User question → LLM chooses a tool → tool runs (Wikipedia / ArXiv / PubMed / Calculator)
             → LLM observes the result → final answer + source links
  • Pattern: ReAct loop on LangGraph with gpt-4o-mini (gpt-4o selectable), the last 6 messages as short-term memory, and optional LangFuse tracing when keys are configured.
  • Tools: Wikipedia and ArXiv through own clients, PubMed through NCBI E-utilities, and a calculator that parses the expression as an AST and never calls eval.
  • Cost and safety limits: question length, per-session and daily token budgets, a recursion limit and escaped HTML.
  • Data: queries are logged to SQLite with tokens and tools used, visible only to the session that made them and kept for 30 days; CSV export is protected against formula injection.
  • Specification first: SPEC.md holds the threat model that the tests below follow.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
95 automated tests run on every push (GitHub Actions, with lint and a dependency audit). The suite needs no API key and no network, so it runs in seconds.

What is verified

  • Security: the calculator rejects code injection and resource-exhaustion input (a test proves a malicious expression never touches the file system); HTML in questions and answers is escaped; Markdown images are stripped from model output; CSV export is protected against formula injection.
  • Agent logic: the real LangGraph agent is driven by a scripted fake model: tool calls, token counting, source collection, the recursion limit and history truncation.
  • Resilience: the Wikipedia, ArXiv and PubMed clients are tested against timeouts, HTTP errors, malformed JSON or XML and XML-bomb input; none of them crashes the agent.
  • Cost control and privacy: per-session and daily budgets, per-session data isolation, SQL-injection strings stay inert, schema migration and 30-day retention.
  • UI: Streamlit AppTest checks rendering, the limits and that one visitor never sees another's history.

Not covered

  • Real calls to OpenAI and the search APIs are verified by hand on the live demo, not in CI.
  • The factual quality of free-text answers is not measured automatically.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The evaluation is small (32 cases, 16 on the dev split run so far), so the confidence intervals are wide and the test split is still unused.
  • Free-text answers can contain errors that no metric here catches; the sources are there so that a reader can check them.
  • Conversation memory is short (6 messages) and the data store is SQLite, which suits a demo and not a multi-user service.

Tech stack: Python 3.11, LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI API, LangFuse, Streamlit, SQLite, Plotly, pandas, pytest, ruff, GitHub Actions.

Related: the Carbon Nanotubes RAG System adds retrieval with a measured answer quality (RAGAs), and the CV Job Matcher uses OpenAI embeddings for semantic ranking.

docs.title: 🔍 SEM Nanostructure Classifier
docs.text:
A classifier for scanning-electron-microscopy (SEM) images of nanostructures, built to answer one question: how much of the reported accuracy is real, once near-duplicate leakage and instrument shortcuts are controlled for?

Live demo: sem-nanostructure-classifier.streamlit.app · GitHub Repository · Weights and model card (Hugging Face)

The Streamlit demo: pick a validation example or upload an image, see the top-3 classes with calibrated probability, an "uncertain" flag below a threshold chosen on validation, and an illustrative Grad-CAM.

docs.title: Why this project
docs.text: Image classifiers on microscopy data often report very high accuracy that does not survive a closer look: the same sample photographed several times lands in both train and test, and the instrument's information bar can carry the label. Instead of chasing a leaderboard score, this project fixes the evaluation rules in a written specification before any code, and then reports what is and is not established — including the negative and inconclusive results.

docs.title: Results at a glance
docs.text:
Test split, group-aware (near-duplicate clusters kept together), mean of 3 seeds:

Model Macro-F1 (95% CI over clusters) Accuracy ECE raw → calibrated ConvNeXt-Tiny 0.956 [0.939, 0.966] 0.972 0.024 → 0.006 ResNet-50 0.944 [0.924, 0.957] 0.965 0.024 → 0.009

Dataset: NFFA-EUROPE "100% SEM Dataset", 10 classes, 20,837 images after removing 332 exact duplicates (CC BY). ConvNeXt-Tiny is ahead of ResNet-50 in every comparison, but this was not tested formally.

docs.title: What the evaluation showed
docs.text:
• Leakage. A random split gives macro-F1 0.968 (ConvNeXt-Tiny) against 0.956 on the group-aware split, a gap of 1.3 pp with the same sign in both backbones; the intervals include or touch zero, so the gap is not established. In the random split 23.4% of test images have a near-duplicate "cluster-mate" in train; these are classified at 99.6-99.9% accuracy, the rest at 96.4-97.2%.
  • Info bar. Removing the bottom 18.75% of every image (where the bar sits) costs 1.4 pp macro-F1 on test (interval +0.4 to +2.3), removing the same amount from the top costs nothing. The validation split shows no drop. Reading: no evidence of a shortcut that carries the classification; a contribution of about 1-1.5 pp in the small classes cannot be excluded.
  • Confidence. Temperature scaling (T = 3.3) cuts the expected calibration error from 0.024 to 0.006. Abstaining below a threshold chosen on validation keeps 94% of test images at 99.2% accuracy (overall 97.2%) and catches about 71% of the errors, but it abstains mostly on rare classes (44% of Porous_Sponge, 37% of Films_Coated_Surface).

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Specification first. SPEC.md fixes the data-security and leakage rules, the split procedure and the test protocol before the code exists; every change is logged in it with a date.
  • Near-duplicate-aware splits. Groups are connected components of cosine similarity ≥ 0.94 between frozen ResNet-50 features; whole clusters go to one of train/validation/test (70/15/15). A test asserts that no cluster crosses splits; thresholds 0.90 and 0.98 serve as a sensitivity check.
  • Fixed configuration, no tuning. One training recipe for every run, 3 seeds per model, epoch chosen on validation macro-F1.
  • Test evaluated once. Each checkpoint touches the test split exactly once, after the configuration was frozen; nothing was changed after seeing test results. The calibration and abstention analysis is post-hoc on stored test logits, with all parameters fitted on validation only.
  • A bug caught before testing. The first group-aware split put almost all large clusters into validation and test. It was noticed from the validation loss, the split was fixed and all group-aware runs were repeated; the details are in the spec.

docs.title: Engineering
docs.text:
• Deployment: Streamlit Community Cloud; the weights live on the Hugging Face Hub and are downloaded on the first start and verified against a recorded sha256 (a mismatch means no model is loaded). Uploads are processed in memory only, nothing is stored or logged.
  • Repository guard: a CI check fails if weights, archives, keys or files over 5 MB are ever committed.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Automated tests run on every push and pull request (pytest and ruff in GitHub Actions). Tests that need PyTorch are skipped without it, and CI runs both variants. No dataset and no trained checkpoint are needed.

What is verified

  • Splits: the near-duplicate groups are built correctly and no cluster crosses the train, validation and test splits.
  • Metrics and calibration: the evaluation and calibration code.
  • Inference: the prediction path of the demo.
  • Download integrity: the weights are accepted only when the sha256 matches.
  • Repository hygiene: no weights, archives, keys or large files tracked.

Not covered

  • The published numbers. Training and the one-time test evaluation ran in Kaggle notebooks that are not in the repository, so CI does not recompute any result; every number comes from a logged run in reports/.
  • Behaviour on images from other instruments or laboratories (there is no external test set).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• One lab, one dataset, no external test set; the group definition (embedding similarity) is a proxy for "same sample".
  • Confidence intervals describe the test sample, not the variation between trainings; with 3 seeds, differences of about 1 pp are at the noise level of single runs.
  • Small classes have 22-46 test images, so per-class numbers move by several points with one image.
  • The demo has no out-of-distribution detector: any image, including a photograph, gets one of the 10 SEM classes.
  • Two ablations from the original plan (class weights, stronger augmentation) were not run.

Tech stack: PyTorch, torchvision (ConvNeXt-Tiny, ResNet-50), Grad-CAM, Streamlit, Hugging Face Hub, pytest, ruff, GitHub Actions.

Related: the same discipline of group-aware splits and honest error analysis, applied to a different domain, is in the Cuneiform Sign Classifier (split by tablet, not by image). A smaller transfer-learning classifier with an honest baseline comparison is the Emotion Recognition project. The nanostructures behind the SEM classes connect to the Carbon Nanotube Visualizer.
